caption: A park ranger at Yellowstone offered me a wheelchair. I was 66 and had ridden 2,000 miles to see Old Faithful. Everybody said it was my age. A retired flight attendant two campsites down proved them wrong.
headline: It Wasn't Her Age. It Was Her Shoes.
script:
A park ranger at Yellowstone asked me if I'd like a wheelchair.

I was sixty-six. I'd ridden two thousand miles in a motorhome to see Old Faithful. And I was on the boardwalk with my shoes off before it went off even once.

On the drive back to the campground, my husband said what everybody says. "Carol, honey. We're not forty anymore."

It took me until the next spring to find out he was wrong. And the answer had been sitting in my closet the whole time.

Let me back up.

I ran a school cafeteria in Dayton, Ohio for twenty-eight years. When we retired, Ray and I made one promise. Every national park we could drive to.

So I did my homework. Hokas, a hundred and sixty-five dollars. Brooks for backup, a hundred and forty. My old Skechers memory foam, seventy, for the campground.

Three pairs. Three hundred and seventy-five dollars. Ray said I packed more shoes than groceries.

None of it mattered. At the Grand Canyon, my arches burned by lunch. The Hokas felt like I was dragging ankle weights up to every overlook.

By Yellowstone, my heels throbbed the second I sat down. My sister, my doctor's nurse, the shoe store lady. They all said it. That's just what happens after sixty.

So at Old Faithful, I sat on that bench with a ranger offering me a wheelchair. And Ray watched the eruption alone.

Then I met Marlene.

She was parked two sites down in Moab the next April. Seventy-one. Retired flight attendant, thirty years standing in an aisle. She'd just hiked eleven miles in Arches.

I asked her what her secret was. She laughed and asked to see my shoes.

She bounced one of my Hokas in her hand. "How many times a day do you lift this?"

I had no idea. "About twenty thousand," she said. "Your legs feel every ounce, every single time."

Then she asked what I do most at a park. I said walk. She said no. "You stand. At overlooks. At visitor centers. Forty-five minutes waiting on a geyser."

A cushioned walking shoe is built to roll you forward. When you stand still, nothing rolls. Your whole weight sits on that soft foam, and it packs down flat.

"Then there's nothing left holding your arch up," she said. "It sinks a little more every minute. That's your burn. That's the heel that throbs when you sit."

Then she asked me. " How much of either one has anything to do with being sixty-six?"

Not one bit of it.

Marlene wanted two things in a shoe. Light enough that you forget it's on. And arch support built into the shoe itself, so there's nothing in there to pack flat.

Hers were Comfort Wear. The Ortho Stretch. About sixty dollars, marked down from a hundred and twenty. I ordered a pair on the campground wifi that night.

The first week, honestly, I didn't trust them. They felt too light to be doing anything. The knit stretched when my feet swelled on long driving days.

Then came Canyonlands. Nine miles. Almost an hour standing in a crowd at Mesa Arch for sunrise. My arches didn't burn. Not hurt less. Didn't hurt.

The grip held on the slickrock. The cushioned sole took the hard ground before my heels did. The wide toe box still had room at mile eight.

This September, we went back to Yellowstone.

Fifty minutes standing on that same boardwalk. Same bench. I never sat on it. When it finally went off, Ray was the one asking where he could sit down.

I was the one asking to stay for the next eruption.

It was never my age. It was three hundred and seventy-five dollars of shoes that were too heavy, or packed flat the minute I stood still.

We drove two thousand miles to see Old Faithful. My husband watched it go off alone.

I was on a bench forty feet back, shoes off, with a park ranger asking if I needed a wheelchair. I was sixty-six. Everybody told me that's just what happens.

Three hundred and seventy-five dollars. That's what I spent on walking shoes for our national parks trip.

Three pairs. Hokas, Brooks, Skechers. And I still spent Yellowstone on a bench. The woman who told me why was parked two campsites down.

caption: There's a framed photo from my 60th birthday trip to New York. My daughters are in it. I'm not. I took it from a bench with my shoes in my lap, and a stranger sitting next to me told me why.
headline: Not Your Age. Your Shoes.
script:
There's a framed photo from my sixtieth birthday. My two daughters at the top of Rockefeller Center, the whole city lit up behind them.

I'm not in it.

I'm the one who took it. From a bench by the elevators, with my shoes in my lap, because I couldn't stand in one more line.

"It's okay, Mama," my oldest whispered. "That's just your age."

She meant it sweetly. She was wrong. And the woman who proved it was sitting on that same bench.

Let me back up.

I'm Paula. Thirty-one years at a bank teller window in Chattanooga, Georgia. Never once been to New York.

So for my sixtieth, Kristen and Amy planned the whole weekend. A Broadway show. The Statue of Liberty ferry. Pizza in Brooklyn. Top of the Rock at sunset.

I bought what every article said to buy. Hokas, a hundred and sixty-five dollars. Then Brooks, a hundred and forty, just in case.

But New York is concrete. Every inch of it. We walked over twenty thousand steps the first day.

And in between, we stood. In line for the ferry. On subway platforms. Outside the theater. Around the block for one slice of pizza.

By the second afternoon, my arches were on fire. My legs felt like sandbags. Every time I sat down, my heels throbbed.

The girls started planning around me. Cabs. Skipping the High Line. I could see it in their faces. Mama's slowing down.

That's how I ended up on that bench at Top of the Rock, holding my shoes in my lap.

The woman next to me was in her late sixties. She glanced at my lap. "Hokas?" I nodded.

Her name was Ruth. She'd led walking tours of Manhattan for twenty-two years. Six hours a day, mostly standing on street corners, talking.

"Honey, it's not your age," she said. "It's two things, and they're both sitting in your lap."

First, the weight. A shoe feels light in the store, she said. But on a city day, you lift it about twenty thousand times. Your legs feel every ounce.

Second, the standing. A cushioned walking shoe is built to roll you forward. In a line, nothing's rolling. Your whole weight sits on that soft foam, and it packs down flat.

"Once it's flat, nothing's holding your arch up," she said. "It sinks a little more every minute you stand. That's the burn. That's the heel that throbs when you sit down."

Then she asked me, "How much of that has anything to do with turning sixty?"

None of it.

Ruth looked for two things. A shoe light enough that you forget it's on. And arch support built into the shoe itself, so there's nothing in there to pack flat.

She stuck her foot out. Comfort Wear. The Ortho Stretch. About sixty dollars, she said, marked down from a hundred and twenty.

I ordered them at the airport gate.

The first week, I wore them around the house, waiting to be disappointed. They felt almost too light. The knit gave a little when my feet swelled by evening.

By the second week, I was walking the mall every morning with my friend Dot. Nothing burned.

Then in December, the girls took me back. A do-over, they called it.

The tree at Rockefeller Center. The Rockettes. A hot chocolate line down the whole block. Nineteen thousand steps on cold concrete.

The grip held on wet sidewalks. My arches held in the last line the same as the first.

My feet didn't hurt. Not hurt less. Didn't hurt.

On the last night, Amy asked, "Mama, you want a cab?" I said no. Let's walk.

There's a new photo on Kristen's wall now. Top of the Rock, all three of us. I'm the one in the middle.

It was never my age. It was a hundred and sixty-five dollars of foam that packed flat the minute I stood still.

My daughters took me to New York City for my sixtieth birthday. By the second afternoon, they were planning the whole trip around my feet.

Cabs instead of walking. Skipping things. "It's okay, Mama. That's just your age." It wasn't. A stranger on a bench proved it in about five minutes.

I spent a hundred and sixty-five dollars on shoes for my sixtieth birthday trip. I spent the best part of it on a bench.

The woman sitting next to me had walked Manhattan for twenty-two years. She looked at the shoes in my lap and said, "Honey, it's not your age."

voice: female, early 70s, warm rural Midwestern (Iowa farm), steady and no-nonsense, a dry laugh in it, grandmotherly

caption: For 31 years I've run the pie booth at our county fair. Last August I quit at noon on day two, and everyone said that's just being 72. Then the woman from the quilt barn picked up my shoe.
headline: It Was Never Her Age
script:
Go to your closet and pick up the shoes you walk in. Just hold them a second. They feel light, don't they?

Now picture lifting them twenty thousand times before supper.

That nearly ended my thirty-one years running the pie booth at our county fair. And it took a woman from the quilt barn to show me it had nothing to do with being seventy-two.

Let me back up.

My name's Bev. Four kids raised on a hog farm outside Ames, Iowa. Eleven grandkids. And every August for thirty-one years, the pie booth in the exhibit hall.

Three days. Fourteen hours a day. Cutting slices, judging the junior bakers, hauling coolers across a concrete floor.

Every summer I buy new shoes for it. Last year, Hokas, a hundred and sixty-five dollars. The year before, Skechers memory foam, seventy. Before that, Brooks, a hundred and forty.

Day one went fine. Day two, by eleven o'clock, my arches were burning. Standing behind that table, my legs felt like they were full of wet sand.

By noon, I told the girls I needed a minute.

My grandson Tyler found me in his pickup with the air running and my shoes on the floorboard. I'd been crying.

That night, my daughter-in-law said it as gently as she could. "Bev, you're seventy-two. Maybe it's time to let somebody else run the booth."

My sister said the same. That's just your age.

Then on day three, Lorraine sat down next to me.

Lorraine runs the quilt barn. She's sixty-nine, and she ran a grocery checkout lane for forty years. Standing in one spot all day.

She looked down at my Hokas and said, "Well, there's your problem. Both of them."

She picked one up. "Feels light, right? But your legs lift whatever this weighs twenty thousand times a day out here. They feel every ounce."

Second, she said, was the standing. And nobody stands like a pie lady.

A cushioned walking shoe is built to roll you forward, she said. Behind a table, nothing rolls. Your whole weight sits on that soft foam, and it packs down flat.

Once it's flat, nothing holds your arch up.

"So it sinks a little further every minute you're standing there," she said. "That's your burn. That's the heel that throbs the second you sit down."

Then she asked me straight. "Bev, how much of either one has anything to do with being seventy-two?"

I didn't have an answer.

Forty years at a register taught her to want two things. A shoe light enough that you forget it's on. And arch support built into the shoe, so there's nothing to pack flat.

Hers were Comfort Wear. The Ortho Stretch. About sixty dollars, down from a hundred and twenty.

Sixty dollars, when the hundred-and-sixty-five-dollar pair had just failed me? I was skeptical. But Tyler ordered them for me that night.

The first week, they felt so light I kept looking down to make sure they were on. The knit gave a little when my feet swelled in the heat.

All spring I wore them. Planting the garden. Standing at my granddaughter's softball games. Nothing burned.

Then August came back around.

Three days. Fourteen hours a day. The cushioned sole took that concrete before my heels had to. The grip held on spilled lemonade.

At four o'clock on day three, my arches felt the same as at seven that morning.

My feet didn't hurt. Not hurt less. Didn't hurt.

On the last night, Tyler came to drive me home before the grandstand show. I sent him to go find us two seats.

Nobody had to cover my booth. I was the one asking to stay for the fireworks.

It was never my age. It was a hundred and sixty-five dollars of foam that packed flat the minute I stood behind that table.
